expect.statement: In adults with moderate or severe PTSD who had stopped their psychiatric medicines (two phase 3 trials from one sponsor: 90 adults with severe PTSD in MAPP1, 104 with moderate to severe PTSD in MAPP2), MDMA given in three sessions within an intensive manualized therapy, compared with an inactive placebo given with the same therapy, reduced clinician-rated PTSD symptoms (CAPS-5, scale 0 to 80, baseline means about 44 and 39) at 18 weeks by 11.9 points more in MAPP1 (95% CI 6.3 to 17.4) and 8.9 points more in MAPP2 (4.1 to 13.7); both arms improved substantially (in MAPP2, by 23.7 and 14.8 points). Among those assessed at 18 weeks, 67% vs 32% (MAPP1) and 71% vs 48% (MAPP2) no longer met PTSD criteria; counting everyone randomized, 61% vs 27% and 70% vs 39% (editors' calculation). Functional impairment improved slightly more with MDMA (SDS difference 1.2 points on a 0 to 10 scale in MAPP2). The two trials share their sponsor, design and therapy manual, and 18 of MAPP2's 19 named authors are also MAPP1 authors; most participants could tell their group and expectancy was not measured, so how much of the difference is due to MDMA itself is uncertain; no outcome after 18 weeks is reported, and no trial compares MDMA-assisted therapy with a trauma-focused psychotherapy. Certainty: moderate. Status: replicated by the same team.
expect.plain: In two trials run for the same sponsor, adults with PTSD had three long therapy sessions with either MDMA or a dummy pill, plus the same talking therapy before and after. About 4 months later, PTSD scores had dropped more with MDMA: about 9 to 12 points more on a 0 to 80 scale. Of the people still checked, about 7 in 10 on MDMA no longer had PTSD, against 3 to 5 in 10 on the dummy pill. Most people could tell which pill they had, so part of the difference may come from what they expected. Nobody has reported what happened after 4 months, and MDMA has not been compared with standard PTSD talking therapy.
expect.population: Adults with DSM-5 PTSD of at least 6 months, CAPS-5 of 35 or more (MAPP1) or 28 or more (MAPP2), after washout of psychiatric medicines; people with current substance use disorders (MAPP1) or most substance use disorders (MAPP2), personality disorders, cardiovascular disease or high suicide risk excluded
expect.magnitude: MAPP1 (de jure MMRM, n = 89): difference 11.9 CAPS-5 points (95% CI 6.3 to 17.4), d 0.91 (0.44 to 1.37); registry least-squares means −24.5 vs −12.64. MAPP2 (n = 103): −23.7 (−26.94 to −20.44) vs −14.8 (−18.28 to −11.28); difference −8.9 (−13.70 to −4.12), d 0.7. Loss of diagnosis among those assessed: 28/42 (67%) vs 12/37 (32%) and 37/52 (71.2%) vs 20/42 (47.6%); with everyone randomized as denominator (editors' calculation): 60.9% vs 27.3% (difference 33.6 points, 14.3 to 52.9) and 69.8% vs 39.2% (30.6, 12.4 to 48.8). Remission 14/42 vs 2/37 and 24/52 vs 9/42. SDS: MAPP2 difference −1.20 (−2.26 to −0.14); MAPP1 P = 0.0116, d 0.43 (−0.01 to 0.88).
expect.grade.reasoning: Two randomized, prospectively registered phase 3 trials (194 analysed in the de facto sets), starting high. Risk of bias, one level: in both trials the outcome-measurement domain of RoB 2 is high, because the CAPS-5, although rated by blinded independent assessors, rests on what participants report, and most participants knew their group (94% on MDMA and 75% on placebo in MAPP2's end-of-study survey; not assessed in MAPP1); expectancy was not measured. A bias of this kind could plausibly account for part of a 9- to 12-point difference but is unlikely to account for all of it, given its size and consistency; rated against the possibility that it explains most of the difference (very serious), the certainty would be low (the strict reading). The de jure estimand drops off-treatment outcomes and placebo dropout was higher in MAPP2 (8 vs 1), but the de facto analyses agree and the likely bias from that dropout runs toward no difference. Inconsistency not rated down: both trials found differences in the same direction with overlapping intervals (d 0.91 and 0.7). Indirectness not rated down because the claim is restricted to the trial populations, to the comparison with placebo plus the same therapy and to 18 weeks. Imprecision not rated down: both intervals exclude no difference, though their lower ends (4.1 and 6.3 points) are small relative to the 10-point change the FDA accepted as clinically meaningful for an individual. Publication bias not rated down: both registered phase 3 trials are published, but all randomized evidence comes from one sponsor, which is why the status is replicated by the same team rather than replicated.

set.grade.domains.risk_of_bias.note: Very serious: unblinding with a participant-reported outcome and no reported measure of expectancy, shared by both trials and of unknown size against differences of comparable order.
set.grade.reasoning: Two randomized, prospectively registered phase 3 trials (193 in the modified intention-to-treat sets, 90 and 103), starting high. Risk of bias, two levels (very serious): in both trials the outcome-measurement domain of RoB 2 is high, because the CAPS-5, although rated by blinded independent assessors, rests on what participants report, and most participants very probably knew their group (in MAPP2's end-of-study survey 94% on MDMA and 75% on placebo identified it, mostly from effects felt or not felt; MAPP1 did not assess blinding and reports only anecdotes); neither trial reports a measure of expectancy, and the assessors' guesses were not recorded. This bias runs toward a larger difference (expectation on MDMA, disappointment on placebo, which the MAPP2 authors themselves name as a possible reason for the 8 vs 1 placebo dropouts, 5 of them after the first session); it is shared by both trials, so their agreement does not reduce it; and its size cannot be estimated from these papers, while the differences it would have to explain are of a comparable order (8.9 and 11.9 points, lower limits 4.1 and 6.3). METHODS §6.3 rates down when the biases that remain could plausibly change the estimate materially, as here; that the bias is unlikely to explain all of the difference argues against very low, not for moderate (the first reader's strict reading; both second readers). The sponsor's oversight of data collection, analysis and interpretation is carried by the status (replicated by the same team), not by a further level. Inconsistency not rated down: both trials found differences in the same direction with overlapping intervals (d 0.91 and 0.7). Indirectness not rated down because the claim is restricted to the trial populations, to the comparison with placebo plus the same therapy and to 18 weeks. Imprecision not rated down: both intervals exclude no difference, though their lower ends (4.1 and 6.3 points) are small relative to the 10-point change agreed with the FDA as clinically meaningful for an individual. Publication bias not rated down: both registered phase 3 trials are published. The relation stays 'reduces': randomization supports causal language about the package that was assigned (MDMA against placebo within the same therapy), which the site uses for randomized evidence at low certainty; how much of the difference is due to MDMA's pharmacology is the question of the contested claim in section 14.

expect.statement: In the two phase 3 trials of MDMA-assisted therapy for PTSD, which compared MDMA with an inactive placebo, most participants could tell which group they were in: in MAPP2, at the end of the study 49 of 52 (94.2%) on MDMA and 33 of 44 (75.0%) on placebo correctly identified their group, most citing effects they felt or did not feel (Bang blinding index 0.92 and 0.55, editors' calculation; 1 means everyone right, 0 chance); MAPP1 did not assess blinding and reports only that at least 9 of 90 participants (10%) had guessed wrongly when told their allocation. The outcome assessors were independent and blinded to treatment and visit, but whether they could guess allocation was not reported, and the primary outcome, a clinician interview, rests on what participants report. Expectancy was not measured in either trial, and the MAPP2 authors' arguments that it was mitigated are indirect. The trials therefore cannot separate MDMA's pharmacological effect from participants' knowledge of their allocation and their expectations: how much of the 9- to 12-point difference reflects these is unknown. Two commentaries that welcomed the trials did not discuss whether the blind held and give no blinding data (Nutt & de Wit, 2021; Madero & Alvarez, 2023), and a 2025 study reports, citing news reports, that the FDA advisory committee raised the difficulty of maintaining the blind given MDMA's psychoactive effects (Earleywine et al., 2025). Certainty: low. Status: single study (MAPP2 is the only trial with a blinding survey).
expect.plain: Both big MDMA trials used a dummy pill with no effects. In the second trial, people were asked at the end which pill they thought they had: 94 in 100 on MDMA and 75 in 100 on the dummy pill guessed right, mostly from what they felt. The first trial did not ask. The people who scored PTSD did not know who had what, but the scores came from what people told them, and nobody measured what people expected. So we cannot tell how much of the extra benefit came from MDMA itself.
expect.magnitude: MAPP2 end-of-study survey: correct 49/52 (94.2%) on MDMA and 33/44 (75.0%) on placebo; wrong 1/52 (1.9%) and 9/44 (20.5%); could not tell 2/52 (3.8%) and 2/44 (4.5%); Bang index (correct minus wrong over all respondents) 0.92 and 0.55 (editors' calculation). MAPP1: not assessed; at unblinding at least 7/44 (15.9%) on placebo and 2/46 (4.3%) on MDMA had believed they were in the other group (anecdotal). Expectancy: not measured in either trial.

expect.statement: In the two phase 3 trials of MDMA-assisted therapy for PTSD (99 people given MDMA and 95 given an inactive placebo, with the same therapy, during about 3 to 4 months of treatment), MDMA compared with placebo increased common, mostly mild or moderate, short-lived adverse events: muscle tightness in 58.5% vs 25.5% (MAPP2) and 61% vs 14% (MAPP1, registry), and more often decreased appetite, nausea, hyperhidrosis, feeling cold, restlessness, mydriasis, bruxism and nystagmus, with transient rises in blood pressure and pulse during sessions. Serious adverse events were rare and occurred only on placebo (2 of 44 in MAPP1, none in MAPP2); severe events occurred in 5 of 53 vs 2 of 51 and mild cardiac events, mostly palpitations, in 7 vs 1 (MAPP2). Suicidal ideation was common in both arms and never rose above baseline; active ideation with some intent emerged in 2 MDMA and 1 placebo participant in MAPP2. No events were coded as misuse or abuse potential. How events were recorded limits these figures: expected effects such as euphoria were deliberately not recorded as adverse events (MAPP1); events were collected by site staff (therapists, in MAPP1), who were probably aware of allocation; relatedness was not assessed except for serious events (MAPP2); attribution to MDMA rested on a twofold difference in frequency; the MAPP1 registry lists substance-use events in 3 vs 0 participants, which the article does not mention; and the trials excluded cardiovascular disease, most substance use disorders and high suicide risk and ended at 18 weeks, too few people and too short to show rare or delayed harms such as later misuse. Two commentaries describe the safety profile favourably without numbers (Nutt & de Wit, 2021; Madero & Alvarez, 2023), and a 2025 study states, citing news reports, that the FDA advisory committee questioned whether the long-term safety data were sufficient and raised therapists' conduct during the trials (Earleywine et al., 2025). Certainty: moderate (for the increase in common adverse events). Status: replicated by the same team.
expect.plain: In two trials, 99 people took MDMA and 95 took a dummy pill, in a clinic, with therapy. MDMA often caused short-lived side effects: tight muscles (about 59 to 61 in 100 people, against 14 to 26 in 100 on the dummy pill), less appetite, sickness, sweating and feeling cold, and blood pressure and pulse went up for a while during sessions. No serious side effects were seen on MDMA; two people on the dummy pill had one. Thoughts of suicide were common in both groups and did not go up. But the trials did not record some expected effects, like feeling very happy, and were too small and short to show rare harms or misuse later on.
expect.population: Adults with moderate or severe PTSD in the two MAPS-sponsored phase 3 trials (MAPP1, 90; MAPP2, 104), excluding cardiovascular disease, most substance use disorders and high suicide risk
expect.grade.reasoning: Two randomized trials, starting high. Risk of bias, one level: adverse events were collected by site therapists who were probably aware of allocation, expected drug effects were deliberately not recorded (MAPP1), relatedness was not assessed and attribution rested on a twofold difference; these affect what was counted, though they could not plausibly create differences as large as those in muscle tightness, appetite, nausea and sweating. Inconsistency not rated down: the same events dominate both trials. Indirectness not rated down because the claim is restricted to the treatment period and the trial populations. Imprecision not rated down for the common events, whose intervals are far from no difference; serious, severe and cardiac events, suicidality and misuse are too few to compare, and the claim says so rather than claiming no increase (METHODS §6.3). Both trials are from one sponsor, hence replicated by the same team.
expect.evidence.14.extracted: MAPP1 reported few serious adverse effects, but trials of phase 3 size without long-term follow-up cannot assess rare events reliably, and such events can emerge once a treatment is in wide use.

expect.statement: As described second-hand in a BMJ news report and two later papers (none of the regulator's own documents was read), the US Food and Drug Administration (FDA) declined in August 2024 to approve Lykos Therapeutics' new drug application for MDMA capsules for PTSD, and according to the company asked for another phase 3 trial. expect.statement: Whether MDMA-assisted therapy for PTSD is cost-effective in the United States has been examined, in the sources read by this reader, only in models funded by the sponsor or co-written by an author who declares financial ties to it, described second-hand in two commentaries; according to the 2025 critique, the answer turns mainly on the comparator and the price of the drug. As described by its critics, the sponsor-funded model compared MDMA-assisted therapy with the same therapy given with a dummy pill (placebo), priced the drug at 36,000 US dollars for the full course, therapy excluded (48,376 dollars for the whole treatment), counted only PTSD-specific health-care costs, drew on 17 months of trial follow-up and found about 84,000 dollars per quality-adjusted life year (QALY) over five years, under its threshold of 150,000 dollars. The critics' own model, whose base-case comparator brings no new costs and no change in health, gave net savings at five years at a lower treatment cost (11,537 dollars); with the sponsor's drug price, payers would break even only after about 8.4 years; and with the drug at 10,500 dollars, about 160 dollars per QALY, with savings below 10,320 dollars. These figures are reported without the model's inputs or any uncertainty range. An earlier model with an overlapping author, quoted in a 2023 commentary, projected 43,000 to 106,000 deaths averted and 109 to 266 billion dollars in net savings over 10 years if 25% to 75% of eligible patients were treated. The critics note that no trial has compared MDMA-assisted therapy with standard PTSD treatments, and no independent economic evaluation is among these sources. Certainty: very low. Status: single study.
expect.plain: Whether MDMA therapy is good value depends mostly on its price and on what it is compared with. The company's study compared it with the same talking therapy plus a dummy pill. Its critics, who also have money ties to the company, say it should be compared with the treatments people would otherwise get, and that at a much lower price it could even save money. No independent study of its value for money was among the papers read.
expect.magnitude: Sponsor's model (second-hand): about 84,000 US dollars per QALY over five years against placebo-therapy, threshold 150,000. Critics' model: net savings at five years at a treatment cost of 11,537 dollars; break-even about 8.4 years at the sponsor's 36,000-dollar drug cost (3.8 years at the lower price of their 2022 analysis); about 160 dollars per QALY at a 10,500-dollar drug price; dominant below 10,320 dollars. Earlier model (second-hand): 43,000 to 106,000 deaths averted, 3.3 to 8.2 million QALYs and 109 to 266 billion dollars in net savings over 10 years at 25% to 75% access. No interval is given for any figure.
expect.grade.reasoning: Modelled projections, not observed outcomes, rated as a description of what the models report (METHODS §6.3): they start low. Risk of bias, one level: every model described comes from the sponsor or from authors with declared ties to it, the critics' new figures are reported without inputs or uncertainty, and none of the models allows for the possibility that the trial effect was inflated by unblinding or expectancy. Indirectness, one level: neither the sponsor's model nor the earlier models were read; their figures are second-hand. The claim states what the result depends on, which the sources show directly, and gives the figures as reported.

expect.statement: Whether the phase 3 trials show that MDMA itself, given within an intensive therapy, is an effective and acceptably safe treatment for PTSD is contested, and the sources read here cannot settle it. Two randomized trials from one sponsor (MAPP1, 90 adults; MAPP2, 104) found larger falls in PTSD symptoms with MDMA than with placebo plus the same therapy at 18 weeks (11.9 and 8.9 CAPS-5 points; see the efficacy claim in section 12) and no serious adverse events on MDMA during treatment. Against this, most participants could tell their group while expectancy went unmeasured; the comparator was placebo, not a trauma-focused psychotherapy; no outcome after 18 weeks is reported; expected drug effects were not recorded as adverse events; in 2024 the US regulator declined approval after an advisory committee most of whose members, as a BMJ news report summarizes its minutes, were not persuaded of effectiveness; and three analyses from the sponsor's phase 2 programme, including the one that set out the rationale for the phase 3 trials, were retracted because the authors had not disclosed protocol violations amounting to unethical conduct at one site, or removed that site's data, and had not fully declared competing interests (the retraction notices). The regulator's own documents were not read. Certainty: low. Status: contested.
expect.plain: Is MDMA, given with talking therapy, a good and safe treatment for PTSD? Not settled. Two trials run for the same sponsor found that PTSD eased more with MDMA than with a dummy pill and the same therapy, over about 4 months, with no serious side effects on MDMA. But most people could tell which pill they had, nobody measured what they expected, MDMA was not compared with standard PTSD talking therapy, and nobody has reported what happened later. In 2024 the US regulator said no, and a journal withdrew three earlier studies from the same programme because rule-breaking at one study site was not disclosed.
expect.grade.reasoning: Rated for the question as posed, which goes beyond what the trials measured. Starting high (randomized trials). Risk of bias, one level, as in the efficacy claim: unblinding with a participant-reported outcome and unmeasured expectancy. Indirectness, one level: the question concerns MDMA's own contribution, durability beyond 18 weeks, comparison with existing psychotherapy and harms in clinical use, none of which the trials measured directly. The short-term comparison with placebo plus the same therapy is rated separately (moderate, section 12). Contested (METHODS §6.4): credible published critiques and the 2024 regulatory events change the interpretation of the trials.
expect.debate.evidence_yes: Two prospectively registered, randomized, placebo-controlled phase 3 trials with central randomization and blinded independent assessors found larger falls in clinician-rated PTSD symptoms with MDMA than with placebo plus identical therapy at 18 weeks: 11.9 points (95% CI 6.3 to 17.4) in 90 adults with severe PTSD and 8.9 points (4.1 to 13.7) in 104 adults with moderate to severe PTSD; 67% vs 32% and 71% vs 48% of those assessed no longer met PTSD criteria (61% vs 27% and 70% vs 39% of everyone randomized, editors' calculation) (Mitchell et al., 2021; Mitchell et al., 2023). The registered primary outcomes are those reported, and analyses that included off-treatment data agreed. The benefit was seen in people with long-standing PTSD, high rates of depression and the dissociative subtype, and again in a more diverse second sample, where only 1 of 53 people stopped treatment on MDMA against 8 of 51 on placebo. No serious adverse event occurred among the 99 people given MDMA; common effects were short-lived and mostly mild; suicidal ideation never rose above baseline in either arm; no events were coded as misuse (Mitchell et al., 2021; Mitchell et al., 2023). The trial's authors argue that phase 3 drug trials are designed to isolate the drug against placebo with the same therapy and that no flawless comparator exists (Mitchell, Coker & Yazar-Klosinski, 2021). A systematic review counted five of six MAPS-linked randomized trials as finding significant benefit (Brett & Bynum, 2025). Two commentaries welcomed the first trial's efficacy and safety, without giving blinding or adverse-event data; one author of each declares an interest in MDMA treatment research or in the sponsor's trials (Nutt & de Wit, 2021; Madero & Alvarez, 2023).
expect.debate.evidence_no: Most participants knew their group: in MAPP2, 94% on MDMA and 75% on placebo identified it at the end of the study, mostly from the effects they felt or did not feel; MAPP1 did not assess blinding; neither trial measured expectancy; and the outcome, although rated by blinded assessors, rests on participants' reports (Mitchell et al., 2021; Mitchell et al., 2023). The MAPP2 authors' arguments that expectancy was mitigated are indirect: five of the eight placebo participants who stopped did so after the first session. Both trials were funded by one sponsor, which designed, analysed and helped write them, and 18 of MAPP2's 19 named authors are also MAPP1 authors (editors' comparison); the review found no randomized trial without a link to MAPS (Brett & Bynum, 2025). The comparator was placebo, not a trauma-focused psychotherapy, and the placebo-with-therapy arm also improved substantially (by 14.8 points in MAPP2); critics argue that a breakthrough claim needs benchmarking against first-line psychotherapies, which on cross-trial figures reach similar effects with half or less of the therapist time (Halvorsen, Naudet & Cristea, 2021). No outcome after 18 weeks is reported. Expected effects such as euphoria were not recorded as adverse events, events were collected by site therapists, and the trials excluded people with cardiovascular disease, most substance use disorders and high suicide risk; the MAPP1 registry lists substance-use events in 3 of 46 participants on MDMA and none on placebo (Mitchell et al., 2021). On 10 August 2024 Psychopharmacology retracted three analyses from the sponsor's phase 2 programme, among them the pooled analysis that set out the design and rationale for the phase 3 trials, because the authors knew of protocol violations amounting to unethical conduct at one site (MP4) when they submitted but neither disclosed them nor removed that site's data, and because competing interests were not fully declared (Mithoefer et al., 2024; Jerome et al., 2024; Feduccia et al., 2024). In August 2024 the FDA declined to approve the application; the BMJ, summarizing the advisory committee's minutes, reported that most members did not think the data showed effectiveness and that all but one judged that the benefits did not outweigh the risks (Mahase, 2024), and news reports cited by a 2025 study describe concerns about maintaining the blind, the long-term safety data and therapists' conduct (Earleywine et al., 2025).
expect.debate.neither_can_show: With an inactive placebo, neither the trials nor their critics can separate MDMA's pharmacological effect from participants' knowledge of their allocation and their expectations, and no trial measured expectancy or the assessors' guesses. Two trials of under 200 people followed for 18 weeks cannot show rare harms, later misuse or durability. No trial compared MDMA-assisted therapy with a first-line psychotherapy, so the cross-trial comparisons of effect sizes and remission rates made by both sides rest on different control conditions and populations. The regulator's own analysis, briefing documents and vote counts were not read, and no source shows whether the problems behind the phase 2 retractions reach the phase 3 data.
expect.debate.editors_reading: Editors' reading (certainty: low). In two trials from one sponsor, MDMA within an intensive therapy led to larger short-term falls in PTSD symptoms than placebo with the same therapy, without serious adverse events on MDMA during treatment (moderate certainty for that comparison; see the efficacy and adverse-event claims in section 12). How much of the difference is due to MDMA rather than to unblinded expectation, whether it lasts beyond 18 weeks, how it compares with trauma-focused psychotherapy and what harms appear in wider use are not answered by the papers read here. The commentaries that first welcomed the trials did not examine the weaknesses on which the later doubts centre. Missing from this reading: the regulator's own briefing documents and decision, the second critique of MAPP1 (Burke & Blumberger, 2021), the trials' supplementary tables and the phase 3 long-term follow-up.

set.debate.evidence_yes: Two prospectively registered, randomized, placebo-controlled phase 3 trials with central randomization and blinded independent assessors found larger falls in clinician-rated PTSD symptom scores with MDMA than with placebo plus identical therapy at 18 weeks: 11.9 points (95% CI 6.3 to 17.4) in 90 adults with severe PTSD and 8.9 points (4.1 to 13.7) in 104 adults with moderate to severe PTSD; 67% vs 32% of completers (MAPP1) and 71% vs 48% of those in the 18-week analysis (MAPP2) no longer met PTSD criteria (61% vs 27% and 70% vs 39% of everyone randomized, for MAPP1 everyone dosed, editors' calculation) (Mitchell, Bogenschutz, et al., 2021; Mitchell et al., 2023). The registered primary outcomes are those reported, and analyses that included off-treatment data agreed. The benefit was seen in people with long-standing PTSD, high rates of depression and the dissociative subtype (in MAPP1, 6 participants on MDMA and 13 on placebo), and again in a more diverse second sample, where only 1 of 53 people stopped treatment on MDMA against 8 of 51 on placebo; in that trial the placebo arm had more women (82% vs 60%), and female sex went with better outcomes in both arms, an imbalance that if anything favours placebo (Mitchell et al., 2023). In the two phase 2 trials in which the systematic review judged the blind maintained or partly maintained, both with a low-dose MDMA comparator, the active doses lowered CAPS scores significantly more than the comparator in one (26 participants) and not significantly in the other (12 participants); these are the review's second-hand accounts of Mithoefer et al. (2018) and Oehen et al. (2013) (Brett & Bynum, 2025). No serious adverse event occurred among the 99 people given MDMA; common effects were short-lived and mostly mild; suicidal ideation never rose above baseline in either arm; no events were coded as misuse (Mitchell, Bogenschutz, et al., 2021; Mitchell et al., 2023). Proponents can also point to longer follow-up: according to two critics of the sponsor's cost-effectiveness model, that model drew on 17 months of follow-up from MAPP2 and its extension study (MPLONG) and documented less health-care use after MDMA treatment, though no outcome figures are given in the sources read (Marseille & Mitchell, 2025). The trial's authors argue that phase 3 drug trials are designed to isolate the drug against placebo with the same therapy and that no flawless comparator exists (Mitchell, Coker, et al., 2021). A systematic review counted five of six MAPS-linked randomized trials as finding significant benefit (Brett & Bynum, 2025). Two commentaries welcomed the first trial's efficacy and safety, without giving blinding or adverse-event data; one author of each declares an interest in MDMA treatment research or in the sponsor's trials (Nutt & de Wit, 2021; Madero & Alvarez, 2023).
set.debate.evidence_no: Most participants identified their group where this was asked: in MAPP2, 94% on MDMA and 75% on placebo identified it at the end of the study, mostly from the effects they felt or did not feel; MAPP1 did not assess blinding; neither trial reports a measure of expectancy; and the outcome, although rated by blinded assessors, rests on participants' reports (Mitchell, Bogenschutz, et al., 2021; Mitchell et al., 2023). The MAPP2 authors' arguments that expectancy was mitigated are indirect: five of the eight placebo participants who stopped did so after the first session. Both trials were funded by one sponsor, which designed, analysed and helped write them, and 18 of MAPP2's 19 named authors are also MAPP1 authors (editors' comparison); a systematic review whose search keywords included MAPS, with no stated way of combining them, found no randomized trial without a link to MAPS (Brett & Bynum, 2025). The comparator was placebo, not a trauma-focused psychotherapy, and the placebo-with-therapy arm also improved substantially (by 14.8 points in MAPP2); critics argue that a breakthrough claim needs benchmarking against first-line psychotherapies, which on cross-trial figures reach similar or greater symptom reductions with half or less of the therapy time (Halvorsen et al., 2021). The trial reports give no outcome after 18 weeks. Expected effects such as euphoria were not solicited as adverse events (MAPP1), events were collected by site therapists, and the trials excluded people with cardiovascular disease, most substance use disorders and (in MAPP2) high suicide risk; the MAPP1 registry lists substance-use events in 3 of 46 participants on MDMA and none on placebo (Mitchell, Bogenschutz, et al., 2021). On 10 August 2024 Psychopharmacology retracted three analyses from the sponsor's phase 2 programme, among them the pooled analysis that set out the design and rationale for the phase 3 trials, because the authors knew of protocol violations amounting to unethical conduct at one site (MP4) when they submitted but neither disclosed them nor removed that site's data, and because competing interests were not fully declared (Mithoefer et al., 2024; Jerome et al., 2024; Feduccia et al., 2024). In August 2024 the FDA declined to approve the application, according to a 2025 commentary citing a CNN report (Marseille & Mitchell, 2025); the BMJ, summarizing the advisory committee's minutes, reported that most members did not think the data showed effectiveness and that all but one judged that the benefits did not outweigh the risks (Mahase, 2024), and news reports cited by a 2025 study describe concerns about maintaining the blind, the long-term safety data and therapists' conduct (Earleywine et al., 2025).
set.debate.neither_can_show: With an inactive placebo, neither the trials nor their critics can separate MDMA's pharmacological effect from participants' knowledge of their allocation and their expectations, and no trial reports a measure of expectancy or the assessors' guesses. Two trials of under 200 people followed for 18 weeks cannot show rare harms, later misuse or durability, and the longer follow-up used in the sponsor's cost model is known here only second-hand, without figures. No trial in the sources read compared MDMA-assisted therapy with a first-line psychotherapy, so the cross-trial comparisons of effect sizes and remission rates made by both sides rest on different control conditions and populations. The regulator's own analysis, briefing documents and vote counts were not read, and no source shows whether the problems behind the phase 2 retractions reach the phase 3 data.
set.debate.editors_reading: Editors' reading (certainty: very low). In two trials from one sponsor, MDMA within an intensive therapy led to larger short-term falls in PTSD symptom scores than placebo with the same therapy, without serious adverse events on MDMA during treatment (low certainty for that comparison and moderate for the rise in common adverse events; see the efficacy and adverse-event claims in section 12). How much of the difference is due to MDMA rather than to unblinded expectation, whether it lasts beyond 18 weeks, how it compares with trauma-focused psychotherapy and what harms appear in wider use are not answered by the papers read here. The two commentaries that welcomed the first trial did not examine the weaknesses on which the later doubts centre. Missing from this reading: the regulator's own briefing documents and decision, the second critique of MAPP1 (Burke & Blumberger, 2021), the trials' supplementary tables, the sponsor's cost-effectiveness analysis and the long-term follow-up of the phase 3 participants (MPLONG).
